Your one focus: **make a slightly fuller shoulder turn going back—without letting your hips sway.**

You already finish in good balance: your trail heel is up, your chest has rotated through, and you’re clearly getting pressure onto your lead side. At the top, though, your lower body stays nicely centered while your arms look like they’re doing a little more of the work than your torso.

Feel your **lead shoulder turn more under your chin** on the backswing, then simply turn through as you are now. That should give you a more connected backswing and easier speed without adding extra effort.

Work on **keeping your chest down through the strike a fraction longer**.

Your head stays fairly centered from address to the top, and you finish with good weight on your lead side and your trail heel up—those are solid. The area to tighten up is avoiding an early lift through the ball; let your chest keep rotating while staying inclined over the ball for a beat longer.

Feel like your belt buckle turns toward the target **while your shirt buttons stay pointed down at the ball** through impact. That should help you strike it more consistently without changing your overall swing shape.

The one thing to work on: **make a wider backswing by keeping your lead (left) arm longer.**

You start in good balance and finish nicely onto your lead foot, so the basic athletic motion is there. But in the backswing, your lead elbow folds early and your hands stay close to your chest. That shortens the swing radius and can make solid contact and speed less consistent.

Feel like your **left hand is reaching away from your chest as your shoulders turn**, rather than pulling the club in around you. Don’t lock the elbow rigidly—just keep it “long.”

A simple rehearsal: make slow backswings stopping when your left arm is about parallel to the ground. Check that your hands are farther from your chest than they are now, then swing through normally.

Work on **turning your chest more in the backswing instead of lifting the club up with your arms.**

At address you have a solid athletic posture and good forward tilt. But early in the takeaway the club gets up quickly and steep while your upper body looks fairly quiet. That can make the downswing overly vertical and force you to rely on timing.

Feel your **left shoulder turn down toward the ball** as your hands move back, with the club staying more in front of your chest—not immediately climbing behind your head.

A simple rehearsal: make slow backswings to lead-arm-parallel, pause, and check that your chest has turned while the club shaft is roughly matching your shoulder angle. Then swing through normally.

**Work on your ball position: it looks too far forward and away from you.**  

You have a solid athletic setup and a nicely balanced finish—your weight gets through to the lead side and you’re holding the finish well. But at address, the ball appears well ahead of your lead foot, which makes your arms reach and can make driver contact and start line less consistent.

For driver, set the ball **opposite your lead heel**, not out past your lead toe. Make a few practice swings feeling that the club bottoms out just behind the ball and brushes up through it.

The backlighting and angle limit the precision a bit, but that setup adjustment is the clearest one visible here.

**Work on a less upright backswing—feel the club swing around you rather than lifting straight up.**

Your address posture is solid, your head stays nicely centered through the backswing, and you finish in good balance. The standout is that at the top your hands and club get quite high and upright relative to where the shaft started. That can make the downswing want to get steep.

Make slow rehearsal swings to waist-high and feel the clubhead staying more *behind* your hands and moving around your body. Then hit easy shots with the thought:

**“Turn the club back around my chest, not up over my shoulder.”**

Don’t force it flat—just slightly less vertical. Your stable posture and balanced finish give you a very good base for that change.

**Work on keeping your lead arm longer through the backswing.**  

You finish in good balance—almost all your weight is on the lead foot—and your posture stays fairly steady at the top. But at the top your arms look quite folded and close to your head, with the lead elbow softening. That shortens the swing radius and can make low-point and strike less consistent.

Feel like your **lead arm stays “long and wide” away from your chest** as the shoulders turn. Don’t lock it rigid; just avoid letting it collapse.

**Simple rehearsal:** make three slow backswings stopping at the top with the sensation that your lead hand is reaching away from your sternum, then hit one ball at 70% speed. Keep the same balanced finish you already have.

**Work on making your backswing less upright—turn the club around you rather than lifting it above you.**

Your setup posture is solid, and you finish in good balance on your lead side. But by the top, your hands and club have lifted very steeply, with the shaft well above the angle it started on. That makes the downswing more timing-dependent.

Feel your **lead arm move across your chest as your shoulders turn**, with the club feeling like it stays more behind your right shoulder—not straight up over it.

A simple rehearsal: make three slow backswings stopping when your lead arm is parallel to the ground. Check that the clubhead is roughly over your hands, not far above them; then hit one normal shot. Keep that as the only thought for now.
